extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, biographers, and educated readers interested in evaluating 17th–18th century literature and lives
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for assessing literary works (especially drama and comedy) and literary biography — what counts as merit, faults, scholarship, and prudence in criticism and defense. Emphasises discriminating judgment, factual accuracy, and sensitivity to genre and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminating censure
rubrics_metrics.description: The censures are not sufficiently discriminating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique should target solid faults and avoid piling on marginal or disputable charges that weaken the overall case. Anti-pattern: accusing an author of additional doubtful offences that invite rebuttal and dilute the critic's authority. Example: Collier weakened his case by including things 'about which there could be the smallest dispute.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish author from dramatic personae
rubrics_metrics.description: One must distinguish between the dramatist and the persons of the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute contempt or irreverence expressed by a character directly to the author's own beliefs; understand characters as rhetorical or dramatic devices. Anti-pattern: blaming Vanbrugh for making Lord Foppington express contempt for church service when that may serve to display character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid professional or personal partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should not be a mere display of professional feeling or claim undue immunity for one's own class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from claiming that members of a particular profession (e.g., clergy) are exempt from ridicule or critique. Beware of extending privileges selectively (e.g., to all religions) as this betrays bias and weakens moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a perfunctory moral couplet as moral redemption
rubrics_metrics.description: A sententious couplet or a moral packed into two or three lines at the end of every play will not undo the mischief that profligate acts have done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral content by the play's overall conduct and effects, not by an appended maxim. Example: Collier showed that Congreve’s supposed morals were insufficient to offset indecencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be judicious in selecting examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid introducing instances which are really quite innocent or slight and can easily be paralleled from writers who served morality and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling evidence, prefer indisputable, representative samples of offense or excellence; including trivial or ambiguous passages undermines the critic's discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance severity with courtesy in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic should temper the rigour of criticism with measured courtesy; when possible 'exchange Balisarda for a less deadly sword' — blunt the point of attack when aiming at a successful and fair review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust tone to the author's circumstances and merits: severe discipline for clear imposture, gentler correction for respected or marginally erring writers. But do not grant blank exemption based on sex or status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific competence in biography
rubrics_metrics.description: No person who is not familiar with the political and literary history of [a period] can possibly write a good life of [a figure from that period].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographers must possess deep, period-specific knowledge (political, literary, social) to portray lives accurately. Anti-pattern: writing from tangential interests (e.g., expertise in Elizabethan matters does not substitute for knowledge of Queen Anne's era).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify dates and facts; careful scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Every paragraph should be revised, and every date and fact about which there can be the smallest doubt will be carefully verified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual accuracy is a baseline requirement for credible biography and criticism; future editions should correct errors and verify doubtful claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authors by their actual strengths and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the subject’s real faculties: e.g., Addison’s proficiency in Latin poetry was 'singularly exact and profound' but his knowledge of Greek and Roman prose was limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should be granular: praise genuine strengths while candidly noting narrower or weaker domains rather than generalising or overstating abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use textual examples to support judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with quotations and concrete textual illustration (e.g., quoting the 'triplet' moral to show inadequacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground evaluative claims in specific passages; anti-pattern is making broad assertions without documentary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of modes of ridicule as a literary virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: All the modes of ridicule, from broad fun to polished and antithetical sarcasm, were at Collier’s command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise or criticize comic writers according to their mastery of comedic modes and tonal variation; versatility in satire and humor is a mark of literary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of honest indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of the rhetoric of honest indignation — eloquence which comes from the heart and goes to the heart — is a commendable quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers who marshal sincere moral passion with rhetorical skill command moral authority. Example: Collier’s energetic eloquence lent weight to his charges despite some errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of distinguishing politics from civic/artistic duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should set aside political prejudices when addressing matters of public taste and morals (e.g., Collier 'forgot that he is a Jacobite, and remembers only that he is a citizen and a Christian').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an author can transcend factional bias to make claims about shared civic or moral standards; this increases persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in taking up public controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should avoid engaging in controversies unsuited to their temper or style — 'it was madness to attempt a vindication' for Congreve to confront Collier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a writer's temperament and rhetorical gifts fit the demands of polemic; poor match (e.g., epigrammatic wit faced with polemical disputant) predicts failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and suitability of polemical style
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful reply in controversy must be clear, lively, and apt; angry, obscure, and dull answers fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate defenses for lucidity, persuasiveness, and appropriate tone. Congreve’s ill-judged reply exemplifies how the wrong style undermines one's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implausible denials and dishonest defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Untruths or implausible denials used in defence are damaging ('to defend himself ... tell untruths which it was certain that nobody would believe!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defense that strains credulity undermines reputation more than it saves it. Prefer candid acknowledgement and contrition when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider social/audience factors in reception
rubrics_metrics.description: A play’s failure on stage does not necessarily reflect its literary merits; audience taste and circumstances matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work's success, separate intrinsic qualities from contingent reception factors (e.g., Way of the World failed on stage despite merits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for life circumstances in assessing later output
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal infirmities, indolence, or changes in habits (e.g., blindness, gout, retirement from stage) affect a writer’s productivity and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical judgment should contextualise late-life writings and output changes; fatigue, illness, or social position can explain shifts in quality or quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the limits of moral apologetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept facile pleas that early follies are excused by later repentance or that youth’s mischiefs should be simply forgiven without demonstrable amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of moral reform critically and demand evidence of sustained change rather than reliance on age or later behaviour alone. Example: Collier asked why Congreve should make the boy’s mischief his own by after-approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate formal and energetic qualities of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Good comedy may require 'constant movement' and 'effervescence of animal spirits' — qualities of pacing and liveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic works for pacing, energy, and vivacity as formal virtues, not only for moral content or polished dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion praise and censure; avoid idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: A man of genius and virtue is but a man; praise should be measured and faults candidly acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographers and critics should resist abject worship of subjects; balanced appraisal fosters credibility. Example: the reviewer refuses 'abject idolatry' of Addison while affirming deserved esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify appropriate dedicatees/patrons in social reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider neutral or representative dedicatees as social-political decisions rather than purely aesthetic ones (e.g., Pope chose Congreve for neutrality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting dedications and patronage, account for political neutrality and social positioning as motives. This helps understand publication strategies and reputational signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate scholarly breadth versus focused mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between deep mastery in one province (e.g., Addison's Latin verse) and cursory acquaintance elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should map an author's intellectual range: praise evident expertise while noting lacunae that might limit their conclusions or translations (e.g., Addison's lack of Greek knowledge affecting annotations).
